title: Composting in a small kitchen
description: Even without a garden, food scraps can become compost instead of landfill with a caddy, a freezer or a community scheme.

body.heading: Why scraps are worth saving
paragraphs: Vegetable peelings, coffee grounds, eggshells and stale bread are not rubbish; they are ingredients. In a compost heap they become food for soil. In landfill, buried without air, the same scraps produce methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.
Many councils now collect food waste separately, which is the easiest route of all: your only job is a caddy on the counter and a bag emptied regularly.

body.heading: Small-space options that work
paragraphs: If you have a balcony or a corner of a garden, a compact compost bin or a wormery handles scraps in very little space and, kept balanced with dry material like shredded paper, smells surprisingly mild.

With no outdoor space at all, try the freezer trick: keep a container of scraps in the freezer, which stops smells completely, and drop it at a community garden or collection point when full. Some neighbourhoods also run shared compost schemes where members take turns.

body.heading: What goes in, what stays out
paragraphs: Fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds and filters, tea leaves, eggshells and plain cardboard make a good mix. Keep meat, fish, dairy and cooked oils out of a home heap, as they attract pests and smell as they break down.
Balance is the whole secret: roughly equal handfuls of wet green scraps and dry brown material like paper or dead leaves. If a heap smells, it almost always needs more dry material and a stir.

takeaway: A counter caddy and a weekly drop-off are enough to turn scraps into soil instead of landfill gas.
